blocks.text: A supermarket display cabinet keeps yoghurt at 4 °C while the shop outside is at 25 °C, moving heat uphill with a compressor that draws only a few hundred watts. The cycle inside is the same vapour-compression loop found in every refrigerator, chiller and heat pump. Its four states can be pinned down from two pressures and a handful of enthalpies.

blocks.markdown: A refrigerator moves heat from a cold space to a warm one by circulating a **refrigerant** that evaporates at low pressure (absorbing heat) and condenses at high pressure (rejecting heat). The ideal **vapour-compression cycle** has four processes on the pressure-enthalpy ($p$-$h$) diagram, where the vapour dome separates liquid, two-phase mixture and vapour.

blocks.title: The ideal vapour-compression cycle
blocks.text: **1→2** isentropic compression of saturated vapour from the evaporating pressure to the condensing pressure; **2→3** constant-pressure heat rejection in the condenser, cooling the superheated vapour to saturated liquid; **3→4** throttling at constant enthalpy ($h_4=h_3$) from condensing to evaporating pressure, producing a liquid-vapour mixture; **4→1** constant-pressure evaporation to saturated vapour, absorbing heat from the cold space.

blocks.caption: Specific heat absorbed, compressor work, heat rejected and coefficient of performance of a refrigerator (per kg of refrigerant)

blocks.title: States and COP of an R134a cycle
blocks.prompt: An ideal R134a cycle evaporates at 0.14 MPa and condenses at 0.80 MPa. Typical property values: saturated vapour at 0.14 MPa has $h_1=239.16$ kJ/kg; isentropic compression to 0.80 MPa gives $h_2=275.39$ kJ/kg; saturated liquid at 0.80 MPa has $h_3=95.47$ kJ/kg. At 0.14 MPa, $h_f=27.08$ and $h_{fg}=212.08$ kJ/kg. Locate state 4, find the quality there and the COP.

steps.text: State 4 is found by throttling: constant enthalpy.
It lies inside the dome; the quality follows from the lever rule.

blocks.answer: State 4 is a two-phase mixture of quality about 0.322, and the ideal COP is about 3.97.

blocks.caption: Cycle states of the ideal vapour-compression refrigerator

blocks.markdown: **Sizing.** The cycle quantities are per kg of refrigerant. The **refrigeration capacity** $\dot Q_L$ (the heat absorbed in the evaporator) fixes the mass flow through $\dot m=\dot Q_L/q_L$. The compressor power then follows from $\dot W_c=\dot m\,w_c$, and the condenser must reject $\dot Q_H=\dot m q_H=\dot Q_L+\dot W_c$. A real compressor has an **isentropic efficiency** $\eta_s=(h_{2s}-h_1)/(h_2-h_1)$, so its real work is larger than the isentropic work, and its discharge enthalpy $h_2$ is higher.

blocks.caption: Mass flow, compressor power and the reversible limit for the same temperatures (absolute)

blocks.title: Sizing the compressor
blocks.prompt: The cycle above must deliver a refrigeration capacity of 10 kW. Find the refrigerant mass flow, the ideal compressor power and the condenser heat rejection. Then repeat the power with a compressor of isentropic efficiency 0.8, and compare with the Carnot COP between 254.3 K and 304.5 K (typical saturation temperatures).

steps.text: Ideal compressor power and condenser load.
Real compressor: the real work is the isentropic work divided by $\eta_s$.
Reversible limit between the same temperatures.

blocks.answer: The flow is about 0.0696 kg/s and the ideal compressor power about 2.52 kW, rising to about 3.15 kW with the real compressor (COP about 3.17). The Carnot value is 5.08, which the cycle correctly stays below.

items: Read or compute $h_1$ (saturated vapour at $p_e$), $h_3$ (saturated liquid at $p_c$) and $h_2$ (isentropic compression to $p_c$).
Throttling is isenthalpic: set $h_4=h_3$ and locate the point under the dome at $p_e$.
Convert to a given capacity with $\dot m=\dot Q_L/q_L$ and $\dot W_c=\dot mw_c$, correcting $w_c$ by the isentropic efficiency for a real compressor.

blocks.title: Why COP is not constant
blocks.text: As the condensing pressure rises or the evaporating pressure falls, the lift $p_c/p_e$ grows: compressor work $w_c$ increases while the refrigerating effect $q_L$ falls (more flash gas after the valve). Both effects lower the COP, which is why running a chiller with a cooler condenser, or a heat pump with a smaller temperature lift, saves energy.

points: The cycle has four states: saturated vapour at compressor inlet, superheated vapour at outlet, saturated liquid after the condenser, and a two-phase mixture after the isenthalpic valve ($h_4=h_3$).
$COP_R=(h_1-h_4)/(h_2-h_1)$ and $\dot m=\dot Q_L/(h_1-h_4)$; compressor power $\dot W_c=\dot m(h_2-h_1)$ is divided by isentropic efficiency for a real machine.
COP is always below the Carnot value for the same reservoir temperatures and falls as the pressure lift increases.

questions.stem: In the ideal vapour-compression cycle, what is the relation between the enthalpy of the refrigerant entering and leaving the expansion valve?

options.text: They are equal, because the throttling process is isenthalpic
The enthalpy falls, because the refrigerant does work in the valve
The enthalpy rises, because the refrigerant evaporates in the valve
The entropy is equal, because the expansion is reversible

questions.correctOptionText: They are equal, because the throttling process is isenthalpic

distractorRationale.b: A throttling valve has no work output and is adiabatic, so the enthalpy cannot fall.
distractorRationale.c: Partial evaporation in the valve uses the refrigerant's own internal energy, not external heat; the enthalpy does not rise.
distractorRationale.d: Throttling is highly irreversible, so entropy increases.

questions.explanation: For steady adiabatic flow through a valve with no work and negligible kinetic energy change, $h_{in}=h_{out}$. The pressure drop causes some liquid to flash to vapour, which is why the exit is a two-phase mixture.

questions.stem: In the standard ideal cycle, the refrigerant entering the compressor (state 1) is:

options.text: saturated liquid at the evaporating pressure
saturated vapour at the evaporating pressure
superheated vapour at the condensing pressure
a two-phase mixture at the condensing pressure

questions.correctOptionText: saturated vapour at the evaporating pressure

distractorRationale.a: Liquid entering the compressor would damage it; vapour is required.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the evaporator exit is saturated vapour at low pressure.
distractorRationale.c: This describes the compressor outlet, not the inlet.
distractorRationale.d: This is not a state in the cycle at that pressure; the valve outlet is two-phase at the evaporating pressure.

questions.explanation: Evaporation completes at the end of the evaporator, so the refrigerant leaves as saturated vapour at the low pressure. The compressor then raises it to the condensing pressure as a superheated vapour.

questions.stem: An ideal refrigerator has $h_1=250$ kJ/kg, $h_2=285$ kJ/kg and $h_3=h_4=100$ kJ/kg. The coefficient of performance is:

distractorRationale.a: Uses the condenser heat over the work, which is the heat-pump COP.
distractorRationale.b: Divides the refrigerating effect by the heat rejected, which is not a COP.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: refrigerating effect divided by compressor work.

questions.stem: A refrigerator has $h_1=251$ kJ/kg, $h_2=283$ kJ/kg and $h_3=h_4=96$ kJ/kg and must provide a refrigeration capacity of 12.0 kW. The ideal compressor power is closest to:

distractorRationale.a: Uses the condenser enthalpy difference in the denominator instead of the refrigerating effect.
distractorRationale.b: Equates the compressor power with the capacity, ignoring the COP.
distractorRationale.c: Multiplies the capacity by the COP instead of dividing.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: mass flow from the capacity, times the specific work.

questions.explanation: The refrigerating effect is $251-96=155$ kJ/kg, so $\dot m=12.0/155=0.07742$ kg/s. The work per kg is $283-251=32$ kJ/kg, giving $\dot W_c=0.07742\times32=2.48$ kW.

questions.stem: A chiller's condenser fouls so that the condensing pressure rises while the evaporating pressure stays fixed. What happens to the cycle?

options.text: The compressor work per kg rises and the refrigerating effect per kg falls, so the COP decreases
The compressor work per kg falls and the refrigerating effect rises, so the COP increases
Both the work and the refrigerating effect rise equally, so the COP is unchanged
Only the refrigerating effect changes, because the compressor work depends on the evaporating pressure alone

questions.correctOptionText: The compressor work per kg rises and the refrigerating effect per kg falls, so the COP decreases

distractorRationale.a: Correct: more work and less refrigerating effect.
distractorRationale.b: Reverses both trends; a higher pressure ratio needs more work.
distractorRationale.c: The effects are not equal: work rises while the refrigerating effect falls.
distractorRationale.d: Compressor work depends on both pressures through the pressure ratio.

questions.explanation: A higher condensing pressure means a larger pressure ratio, hence more work $h_2-h_1$. The saturated liquid also has a higher enthalpy $h_3$, so $h_4$ rises and $q_L=h_1-h_4$ falls. Both changes lower $COP_R$.

questions.stem: An ideal vapour-compression cycle has $h_1=238$ kJ/kg, $h_2=272$ kJ/kg and $h_3=h_4=92$ kJ/kg. Find the coefficient of performance of the refrigerator.
A refrigeration plant must provide 25.0 kW of cooling. The cycle has $h_1=240$ kJ/kg, $h_2=268$ kJ/kg and $h_3=h_4=88$ kJ/kg. Find the ideal compressor power in kW.
questions.explanation: The refrigerating effect is $240-88=152$ kJ/kg, so $\dot m=25.0/152=0.1645$ kg/s. The compressor power is $\dot m(h_2-h_1)=0.1645\times28=4.605$ kW.

questions.stem: A refrigerator has $h_1=239$ kJ/kg, isentropic discharge enthalpy $h_{2s}=271$ kJ/kg and $h_3=h_4=95$ kJ/kg. The compressor has isentropic efficiency 0.75. Find the actual COP of the refrigerator.
questions.explanation: The isentropic work is $271-239=32$ kJ/kg, so the actual work is $32/0.75=42.67$ kJ/kg. The refrigerating effect is $239-95=144$ kJ/kg, giving $COP=144/42.67=3.375$, lower than the isentropic value 4.5.

questions.stem: Sketch in words the ideal vapour-compression cycle on a pressure-enthalpy diagram and show how you locate each of the four states from a given evaporating pressure and condensing pressure. State the process type linking each pair of states.
markingGuide: State 1: saturated vapour on the right-hand side of the dome at the evaporating pressure
1 to 2: isentropic compression, moving up and to the right along a line of constant entropy to the condensing pressure; state 2 is superheated vapour
2 to 3: constant-pressure heat rejection, a horizontal line to the left through desuperheating and condensation to saturated liquid at the left of the dome
3 to 4: isenthalpic throttling, a vertical line down to the evaporating pressure, ending inside the dome (two-phase)
4 to 1: constant-pressure evaporation, a horizontal line to the right
Mentions that quality at 4 follows from the lever rule and that the two horizontal lines are the pressure levels
questions.explanation: On the $p$-$h$ diagram the two pressures give two horizontal lines. State 1 is where the low-pressure line meets the saturated vapour curve, state 3 where the high-pressure line meets the saturated liquid curve. State 4 is directly below state 3 (constant enthalpy), and state 2 is on the high-pressure line along the isentrope through state 1.

questions.stem: Explain why the coefficient of performance of a refrigerator cannot exceed the Carnot value and why a real cycle has a lower COP than the ideal cycle on the same evaporating and condensing pressures. Relate your argument to the quantities $q_L$, $w_c$ and the compressor isentropic efficiency.
markingGuide: COP_R = q_L/w_c and the Carnot COP = T_L/(T_H - T_L) is the maximum for reservoirs at T_L and T_H (second law)
Ideal cycle is below Carnot because heat rejection takes place with superheated vapour and throttling is irreversible (flash gas reduces refrigerating effect)
Compressor isentropic efficiency below one means actual work w_real = w_s/eta_s, larger than the ideal work
Actual COP = q_L/w_real is lower, and discharge enthalpy h_2 is higher so more heat is rejected
Pressure drops in heat exchangers and pipes and superheating at the compressor inlet further reduce performance
Capacity sizing: for a given Q_L the compressor power rises as w_real increases
questions.explanation: The second law limits any refrigerator between two reservoirs to the Carnot COP. The vapour-compression cycle loses further to irreversible throttling and superheated heat rejection, and a real compressor needs $w_s/\eta_s$ of work. With the same refrigerating effect, the extra work lowers the COP.
